To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) the ultimate parallel computer consists of an infinite square mesh of synchronous area-universal modules, and (b) its speed is bounded by the speed of light and the number of processors.
the ultimate parallel computing machine is a bounded-size, synchronous, area-universal, square-mesh machine, with the speed of light and the device size as its only physical limitations.
the physical bounds on parallel machines are the square mesh, the bounded-size synchronous module, and the processor-time tradeoff.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental understanding of the ultimate impact of physical limits, and not with their actual achievement.
the ultimate limits of parallel computing and the implications of these limits for the design of future parallel machines.
the fundamental limits on the performance of parallel computing machines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the ultimate parallel computing architecture is a two-dimensional square mesh, where the number of processors is the square of the number of dimensions, and where the number of dimensions is the number of bits per word.
, in a sense, Moore's law will continue to hold.
, in the limit, parallel computing is a local phenomenon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, although the physical limitations do not preclude scalability, the latter is possible only for a restricted class of interconnection topologies.

, although the physical bounds are severe, they can be met with a modest number of processors and with a modest speedup, but with a large number of memory modules and a large memory access time, and that, although latency-hiding is not possible, it can be made tolerable.
parallel computing is not doomed by physics, but that its future will be radically different from the past.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ultimate physical limitations on the speed and size of computing modules are likely to be a major factor in the design of future parallel machines.

, as the technology advances, we will be increasingly forced to abandon the traditional processor-centric view and to embrace a more holistic view of the computing system, where the interconnect and memory are equally important.
the physical limits on computing are much more severe than those on communication, and that the ultimate parallel computer is very different from what we are used to.
